title: Longest Uncommon Subsequence I
statement:
Two strings `a` and `b` are given. A string is an *uncommon subsequence* of the pair when one of `a`, `b` contains it as a subsequence and the other does not. A subsequence of `s` is what remains after deleting zero or more characters of `s` without reordering the rest, so `s` itself counts.

Return the greatest length an uncommon subsequence of `a` and `b` can have, or `-1` if the pair has no uncommon subsequence.
constraints: a and b consist of lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

The brute force lists every subsequence of both strings and keeps the longest one found in only one of them, which takes O(2^n) time. A single observation makes that unnecessary: the longest subsequence of a string is the whole string.

- If `a` and `b` are equal, every subsequence of one is a subsequence of the other, so nothing is uncommon.
- Otherwise take the longer string (either one if the lengths match). It cannot be a subsequence of the other string: a subsequence is never longer than its source, and one of the same length would have to be the whole source, which is a different string. No uncommon subsequence can be longer than the longer string, so its length is the answer.

## Approach

1. If `a === b`, return `-1`.
2. If the lengths differ, return the larger one: the longer string does not fit inside the shorter.
3. Otherwise the strings have equal length but differ, so return `a.length`: `a` is a subsequence of itself but not of `b`.

## Example 1, step by step

`a = "aba"`, `b = "cdc"`. The strings differ, and both have length 3, so the reference reaches the last line and returns `3`: `"aba"` is a subsequence of `a` but not of `"cdc"` (and `"cdc"` works just as well).

## Complexity

- Time: O(min(|a|, |b|)) for comparing the two strings; the rest is O(1).
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- When one string is a subsequence of the other, the answer is still not `-1`: for `"abc"` and `"ab"` it is 3, because `"abc"` does not appear in `"ab"`.
- Strings of equal length that differ still give that length, even if they use the same letters (`"abcd"` and `"abdc"`).
- There is no need for a longest common subsequence or any character counting.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `a`, `b` | the two input strings; only their equality and lengths matter |

narration.2: Identical strings share every subsequence, so nothing is uncommon.
narration.3: Report that no uncommon subsequence exists.
narration.5: Different lengths: the longer string cannot be a subsequence of the shorter one.
narration.6: So the whole longer string is the longest uncommon subsequence.
narration.8: Same length but different: a is a subsequence of itself and not of b.
